title: The Galactic Centre above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope
caption: The Galactic Centre above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla is at work, its dome lit by the Moon. Across the frame runs the Milky Way, our galaxy, a disc seen perfectly edge-on. Above the dome, partly hidden by dark dust clouds, bulges the galaxy's prominent yellowish centre.

The galactic plane holds a hundred thousand million stars along with a great deal of interstellar gas and dust. The dust absorbs visible light and re-emits it at longer wavelengths, so to our eyes it looks completely opaque. Ancient Andean civilisations saw animal-shaped constellations in these dark lanes. Follow the lane that seems to grow upward from the galactic centre and you arrive at Antares (Alpha Scorpii) and the reddish nebula surrounding it.

The Galactic Centre sits in Sagittarius and is best seen during the southern winter. The telescope, inaugurated in 1976, now works with the HARPS spectrograph, which ESO calls the world's most precise exoplanet hunter.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Serge Brunier. The source does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The dust lanes are opaque to the eye in visible light, and a camera gathering light over time may show the yellowish bulge and the reddish nebula more vividly than an observer would see them.

explore: La Silla lies on the outskirts of the Chilean Atacama Desert, 600 km north of Santiago and 2400 m above sea level. It was ESO's first site in Chile and was the largest observatory of its time. ESO Photo Ambassador Serge Brunier took this photograph.
alt: The Milky Way running edge-on across the sky, with its yellowish central bulge partly hidden by dark dust above a moonlit telescope dome.
